title: From blocks to Action rows
summary: By the end of [[build-programs]] a matcher has produced a `Block` carrying a `data` dict. This chapter is the last leg: how that block becomes an `Action` row with an id, a time window, a tx-hash set, an accounts set, eight directional columns and one protocol-specific composite. Two files do the work. `ClassifyCore.cpp` runs the post-pass stage — the host post-processors (`post_process_dedust_liquidity`, `post_process_stonfi_v2_liquidity`, `unwind_deployments`) that mutate the already-matched block set, plus the per-trace exception boundary that decides between "commit these actions" and "throw them all away and fall back to leaf actions". `ActionBuild.{h,cpp}` is the `block_tree_serializer.py` port: `build_action` fills the universal fields, `fill_action` dispatches on btype to one of 21 `fill_*` functions. Rendering is NOT in either — `render_action` stays harness-side in `Classify.cpp`, which is the whole point of the core/harness split. Two things will surprise you if you know the Python classifier from another branch: there is NO role system on this branch (`action_accounts` is role-less by design, not by omission), and the A/B twin gate compares FULL rendered rows, so every field you see below is byte-pinned against the real Python serializer over 148 fixtures.

sections.heading: The seam: a CoreAction is not a row
sections.prose:
The core deliberately stops one step short of an `Action`. What the matcher loop collects is a `CoreAction`: four raw pointers into the caller's arena, no strings, no rendering, no schema. Everything that turns those pointers into text or into a row happens in an adapter — the CLI dump in `Classify.cpp`, or the production actor in [[prod-path]].

That sounds like ceremony until you notice WHEN a CoreAction is collected versus when it is rendered. It is collected at fire time, mid-walk, while later matchers are still mutating the tree; it is rendered after the post-pass, from the block's FINAL state. Keeping the two apart is what lets a later merge rewrite `produced->data` and have the row reflect it.

excerpts.title: CoreAction / ClassifyResult — the core's whole output vocabulary

annotations.text: `anchor` and `produced` are usually different blocks: the anchor is where the matcher's `test_self` hit (the block whose key the dump prints), `produced` is the new composite block the match built. On the fallback path they are deliberately the SAME pointer — a leaf block is its own anchor.

`aux` is the one piece of fire-time state that cannot be recovered later. It is captured from the anchor's `next_blocks` at match time; by the time the post-pass has run, merges may have moved those siblings. Storing them as raw pointers (not rendered strings) is what keeps the core rendering-agnostic while still preserving the fire-time answer.

"Buffered ATOMIC" is the contract that makes the failure fork possible: nothing is printed or inserted while the trace is being classified, so a throw halfway through can discard the whole trace's output without needing to un-emit anything. Python gets this for free by building a list; C++ has to promise it.

Two separate action vectors, never both populated. `fallback_actions` is the Step 2c path and is UNGATED — no corpus trace fails, so the A/B twins never exercise it. Treat any behaviour you read in `basic_classify_fallback` as unproven-by-gate, unlike everything else on this page.

excerpts.title: Where aux comes from (end of try_build)

annotations.text: Read from the ANCHOR's `next_blocks`, not the produced block's. The merge just consumed a set of blocks into `produced`, but the anchor's sibling list is untouched by that — so excess/bounce messages that trail the matched subtree are still visible here and only here.

`stable_sort` by `min_lt` before scanning: the list is already in canonical order ([[block-tree]]), but the sort is re-asserted because `aux` order IS rendered and a merge earlier in this same walk could have appended out of order.

Two hardcoded opcodes — `0xD53276DB` (excess) and `0xFFFFFFFF` (bounce) — gated per matcher by `include_excess` / `include_bounces` from the IR ([[ir-artifact]]). A matcher that opts out simply gets an empty aux list; the messages stay unconsumed in the tree.
The only place a CoreAction is created on the normal path. Note what is NOT stored: no data snapshot, no rendered strings. `produced->data` is read later, after the post-pass may have rewritten it.

sections.heading: The post-pass stage: what survives becomes a row
sections.prose:
After every matcher has walked, three host post-processors run over a freshly re-collected spine list. They are ports of `blocks/liquidity.py` and `event_processing.py`, and unlike matchers they are imperative surgery on the block graph: they merge two produced blocks into one, re-parent children, and delete blocks that already have a CoreAction pointing at them.

That last part is the mechanism to understand. A post-processor never touches `pending`; it inserts into a `removed` set, and the filter at the end of `classify_trace` is what actually drops the row. So "this matcher fired but produced no action" has exactly two causes on this branch: a clean rejection inside `try_build` ([[matcher-runtime]]), or a post-processor merging the produced block away here.

excerpts.title: The pass chain and the survival filter

annotations.text: The spine is re-collected from scratch AFTER matching, not reused from the prefilter inventory at the top of the function. It has to be: matchers rewired `next_blocks` as they merged, so the pre-match BFS order is stale. Note the walk follows `next_blocks` only — children of produced composites are not on the spine.

Order is load-bearing and mirrors `event_processing.py` exactly. `post_process_stonfi_v2_liquidity` pairs blocks that `post_process_dedust_liquidity` may already have merged; running them the other way round changes which pair survives. `unwind_deployments` last, and it is a no-op for the dumps (it only appends to the spine, which the dump never re-walks) — ported so the chain matches production, per [[prod-path]].

The whole survival rule in three lines, and it keys on `produced`, not `anchor`. A merged-away block's CoreAction disappears silently — there is no "merged" marker in the output, the row just isn't there. When a dump has fewer rows than you expect, this filter and `try_build`'s clean rejection are the two places to look.

excerpts.title: post_process_dedust_liquidity — merge two blocks, delete one

annotations.text: `contract_key` deliberately uses `describe()` (the debug rendering) for anything that is not an Account. That is not sloppiness: the key only needs to group blocks, and Python groups by the raw object's equality. Using `describe()` gives a total, deterministic key for the Null / wrong-type cases without adding a branch per Value kind ([[value]]).

Python logs a warning and skips merging when a deposit contract appears more than twice; C++ silently returns. The stdout channel is the A/B comparison channel, so a log line here would be a diff — warnings that Python prints to its logger have no C++ counterpart by design.

`combine_deposits` signals its consistency failures by throwing, and the catch turns that into "leave the pair unmerged" — the net effect of a Python `raise` propagating out of the same call. Unreached over the corpus, so this is parity by construction rather than by gate.

The merge itself: `first` is erased from the spine AND inserted into `removed` (two different jobs — the spine erase affects later passes, the `removed` insert kills the row), then its event nodes and children are folded into `final_b` and the lt window recomputed. The `sort`+`unique` on `children_blocks` is a pointer-value dedup, which means child order after a merge is ADDRESS order, not lt order — harmless only because `emit_action` sorts the rendered child keys.

excerpts.title: unwind_deployments — the loop that must see its own appends

annotations.text: The honesty note that matters: this pass is a no-op for both dumps. It appends promoted `contract_deploy` blocks to the spine, and the dump emits matcher-produced blocks from `pending`, never the spine. It exists so the pass chain is identical to production, where the spine IS the serialization input.

An index loop, not a range-for, and the comment says why: Python's `for block in blocks` over a list being appended to re-scans the appended entries. A range-for (or a cached `end()`) would silently change the traversal — and because the pass is a dump no-op, the gate would not catch it.

Note the else: a promoted deploy's own children are NOT queued. Promotion terminates the descent on that branch, so a deploy nested inside a deploy is reached on the outer loop's later pass over the appended entry, not here.

sections.heading: The failure fork
sections.prose:
`classify_trace` wraps the whole matcher loop and post-pass in one try/catch. This is the C++ image of `event_processing.py`'s per-trace boundary: a trace that throws anywhere loses ALL its classified actions and is re-run through a leaf-only classification instead.

The `FailureCategory` enum next to it is newer and serves a different purpose — shadow-mode telemetry for [[prod-path]]. It is worth reading its comment carefully, because it documents as much by what it refuses to enumerate as by what it does.

excerpts.title: FailureCategory — four members, and the argument for four

annotations.text: "TRACE-TERMINAL reasons only" is the type invariant. The field holds ONE value for a whole trace, so anything that can happen many times per trace (a clean reject, a null parse, a lookup tier miss) cannot be a member without making the type lie.

`malformed_trace` is the one member `classify_trace` never sets — the trace never reached it. It is set caller-side by whoever failed to build the event tree ([[block-tree]]), which is why you will not find it assigned anywhere in `ClassifyCore.cpp`.

The deliberately-excluded list. `matcher_skip` is a SETUP fact (read from `ClassifySetup.skips`, same for every trace) and would be a category error here; the per-lookup misses are counted separately in `LookupStats`. This comment is the reason the enum shrank from a larger draft to four.

Categorisation by substring match on the exception message. Fragile-looking, and it is — the string `"two-phase lookup did not converge"` is thrown by the build driver and matched here by text. It survives because the category is telemetry only: getting it wrong mislabels a metric, it does not change a row. Anything else is `engine_fault`.

The catch-all is NOT redundant. A parser tail can throw something that is neither a `std::exception` nor a `vm::VmError` ([[parse-layer]] covers the narrow catch list one level down); without this the throw would escape into the caller's loop and take the whole corpus run with it.

`actions.clear()` is the atomicity promise being kept: a trace that failed at action 40 does not emit its first 39. Python does the same by letting the list go out of scope. The fallback is then computed from a FRESH block tree, not from the half-mutated one — see the next excerpt.

excerpts.title: basic_classify_fallback — a second classification with no matchers

annotations.text: `init_block` over `ctx.tree.root` again: a brand-new spine, allocated from the same arena, sharing nothing mutable with the tree the failed run mangled. That is the only safe thing to do — the failed run threw mid-merge, so the old spine may be half-rewired.

The post-processor chain runs here too, over blocks no matcher ever touched. In practice they all no-op (there are no dedust/stonfi composite btypes without matchers), but the chain is kept verbatim because Python's `try_classify_basic_actions` calls it.

The `serialize_blocks` skip conditions, inlined: root/empty wrappers out, and a `call_contract` with a null source OR destination out. That second rule is why a bounced-to-nowhere message never becomes a fallback row.

`CoreAction{"basic", b, b, {}}` — anchor and produced are the same block, matcher_name is the literal `"basic"`, aux is empty. Downstream `build_action` cannot tell the difference, which is exactly why the fallback rows render through the same code path. The catch-all `out.clear()` reproduces Python's "fallback returns [] on any exception": a failure to fall back yields no rows at all, never a partial set.

sections.heading: build_action: the fields every row gets
sections.prose:
`ActionBuild.{h,cpp}` moved out of the harness in R1b so the production actor could call it without dragging stdout printing along. The code is byte-identical to what used to live in `Classify.cpp` — the twin dumps proved the move.

`build_action` fills what does not depend on btype: the action id, the lt/utime window, `mc_seqno_end`, `tx_hashes`, and `accounts`. Then it calls `fill_action`, and only if that succeeds does it assemble accounts — because accounts are derived from the directional fields the fill just wrote.

One honesty note about the demo trace used below (`013-itRDy…`): in PRODUCTION this trace is classified as `coffee_staking_claim_rewards` — the coffee staking protocol is NOT ported to mch specs, so the mch engine (both C++ and its Python twin, identically) classifies the ported jetton_transfer leg instead. The row is real and every column below is exactly what ActionBuild emits; it is just not what the production classifier stores for this trace. The twin gate proves C++ == Python-mch over PORTED specs — not C++ == the production event_classifier. See [[gates]] for the precise claim.

excerpts.title: The Action struct — a flat, fixed schema

annotations.text: THE divergence from the docs you may have read. `accounts` is a bare `vector<string>` with no parallel role map, because this branch has no role system: `action_accounts` in `indexer/core/database.py` is `(action_id, trace_id, account)` plus lt/utime denormalisation and NOTHING else, and `role_assignment.py` does not exist here. CLAUDE.md's ROLE_SENDER/ROLE_RECEIVER section describes a different branch. Verified in "Check yourself" below.

Eight directional columns + `amount`/`value`/`opcode`, all typed `Value` rather than `string`/`int64`. That is not laziness: it gives "unset" a first-class representation (`Null`) distinct from empty-string, matching Python's `None` exactly, so a field the fill never touched renders as `null` on both sides.

Fourteen composite columns, one per protocol family, plus `extra`. A new action type is supposed to REUSE one of these rather than add a column — `fill_dedust_v2_claim_reward` below is the worked example of that rule, and it is why the list has stayed this length.

excerpts.title: build_action head — id, time window, tx_hashes

annotations.text: The action id is `base64(sha256(msg_hash_or_tx_hash + btype))` over the EARLIEST event node. The tie-break is load-bearing: `n->lt() < root->lt()` with strict `<` keeps the first minimum, which is what Python's `min()` returns. Flip it to `<=` and traces with two nodes at the same lt get a different id — a silent, data-dependent diff.

`end_lt` / `start_utime` / `end_utime` / `mc_seqno_end` are recomputed here from `event_nodes`, whereas Python reads `block.max_lt` / `min_utime` / `max_utime`. They agree because Python's `calculate_min_max_lt` computes them from the same node set — but the C++ `Block` genuinely has no such fields ([[block-tree]]), so this is a re-derivation, not a read. `node_utime` (above, line 86) reproduces `get_utime`'s three-way rule: tick_tock -> tx.now, created_lt set -> created_at, else tx.now.

Every accumulator is null-guarded on `n->tx`. Python is not: `max(n.message.transaction.lt ...)` would raise on a tick_tock node and `max(...)` over an empty `event_nodes` raises ValueError. The guards below (`event_nodes.empty() ? 0 : …`) make the C++ total where Python would throw — unreachable for the ported btypes, but it means a bug here degrades to a zero rather than to a trace failure.

The Step 2a extension: the block's `initiating_event_node` contributes its tx hash even though that node is not in `event_nodes`. `std::set` gives sorted-unique for free; Python uses `set()` and gets arbitrary order, which is why BOTH dumps sort `tx_hashes` before rendering. Do not read meaning into the order.

excerpts.title: build_action tail — the accounts set (no roles)

annotations.text: Accounts are assembled AFTER the fill, and that ordering is required: three of the four sources below are the directional fields the fill just wrote. A fill that forgets to set `source` silently shrinks the accounts set — which is a missing `action_accounts` row in production, not a visibly wrong column.

`push_acc` accepts only `VType::Str`. That works because `av_addr` has already converted every Account/Asset to a canonical string — a directional field still holding an `Account` would be silently dropped. The invariant "directional columns are Str or Null" is enforced by convention in the fills, not by the type.

The `is_ghost_block` gate on destinations. On this branch the C++ substrate has no ghost nodes so the flag is always false (see `BlockTree.h`), meaning this branch is structurally dead — ported anyway because the Python serializer has it and a future ghost-producing matcher would need it.

The initiating tx's account joins the set unless the node is tick_tock. Python logs a debug line when that account was not already present; C++ does not (stdout is the diff channel). `sort`+`unique` versus Python's `list(set(...))`: the CONTENTS are gated, the order is not — both dumps sort, and `action_accounts` is a set of rows anyway.

sections.heading: fill_action: dispatch, helpers, and two representative fills
sections.prose:
Everything btype-specific lives in a `fill_*`. They all have the same shape: read `block.data` fields by name, run them through one of three converters, write directional columns and one composite dict. The converters are the interesting part — they are where the engine's rich `Value` types ([[value]]) collapse into the flat column types the DB expects.

One consequence worth internalising before reading any fill: `render_value` SORTS dict keys, so the order of `f.emplace_back(...)` calls is invisible to the A/B gate. The names and values are pinned; the emission order is not.

excerpts.title: The three converters every fill runs on

annotations.text: `av_addr` is the whole reason directional columns render as `str:0:ABC…` and not `asset:…` or a raw Account. Note the two null-producing cases: an `Asset` with no jetton (i.e. TON) becomes Null, and an `addr_none` Account becomes Null. So "TON" and "no address" are indistinguishable in a column — a fill that needs to say "this leg was TON" has to encode it elsewhere (see `fill_jetton_transfer`'s asset branch).

`av_amount` unwraps `Amount` to its underlying Int (or Float for the NaN-ish cases), and passes a bare Int through untouched. That passthrough is what lets jvault/evaa/tgbtc fills, whose builders emit raw ints rather than Amounts, share the same converter. It also means you cannot tell from the row whether the builder produced an Amount.

`dg` returns Null for a missing key, `has` distinguishes missing from present-and-null. Several fills need BOTH (`has(d,"receiver_wallet") ? av_addr(...) : Null` in the next excerpt) because the Python side reads the key conditionally — the same conditionally-present-key discipline as the parse layer ([[parse-layer]]), one level up.

excerpts.title: fill_jetton_transfer — the row from the run above

annotations.text: `has(...)` guarding a field that `dg` would already return Null for. It is not redundant in intent: it documents that Python reads `receiver_wallet` only when the builder set it. Since both branches produce Null here, this is one of the few places where the C++ is defensive beyond what the gate can prove.

The TON-vs-jetton fork. A TON `Asset` becomes Null explicitly rather than by falling through `av_addr` — semantically the same result, written out because the reader needs to know that `asset=null` on a jetton_transfer row means TON, not "unknown".

The composite. Seven keys, and two of them (`custom_payload`, `forward_payload`) are Cell-derived — they render as `cellhash:HEX` rather than as serialized BOC, which is the §12 root-hash bar that makes pytoniq-vs-td serialization differences invisible to the byte diff. `comment` goes through `comment_value`, which picks base64 for encrypted comments and UTF-8 backslashreplace otherwise.

excerpts.title: fill_dedust_v2_claim_reward — reusing a composite instead of adding one

annotations.text: The T12.2 protocol from [[parse-layer]], arriving at its final destination. Note what it does NOT do: set `a.type`. The row's type stays the raw btype `dedust_v2_claim_reward` — several other fills DO rewrite type (`fill_dedust_deposit` -> `dex_deposit_liquidity`, `fill_ethena_deposit` -> `stake_deposit`), so the btype and the rendered type are not interchangeable.

A reward claim is modelled as a one-sided liquidity withdrawal: every side-2 key is explicitly Null rather than omitted. Emitting the nulls (instead of leaving keys out) is what keeps the composite's key SET constant across the btypes that share it — the DB composite is positional, so an absent key and a null key are not the same thing downstream.

Worth a look before this reaches production: `is_refund` is emitted by both engines (Python's `_fill_dedust_v2_claim_reward` sets it too, so the A/B gate is satisfied), but the `dex_withdraw_liquidity_details` CompositeType declared in `indexer/core/database.py` has no such column. The gate proves the two engines agree on the dict; it says nothing about what Postgres stores.

`extra` is the escape hatch for the one field that fits no existing composite. Preferring `extra` over a new column is a standing rule on this branch — a new composite type means a DDL migration on a table with billions of rows.

excerpts.title: fill_action — the dispatch, and what is deliberately missing

annotations.text: An if/else-if chain on `b->btype`, matching Python's `match block.btype`. The Python version has ~90 cases; this has 21. The difference is not a porting backlog — it is the corpus: only btypes that FIRE in the fixture set can be A/B-gated, and an ungated fill is a liability.

`contract_deploy` shares `fill_call_contract`, exactly as Python's `case 'call_contract' | 'contract_deploy'` does. Both are fallback-only here: the main dump's blocks are matcher-produced composites, never leaves.

The only fill that takes a third argument. `evaa_withdraw` derives `success` from BOTH the data's `is_success` field and the block's `failed` flag — the one place where a row's success is not simply `!b->failed`.

The named skip, and the honest reason: `nft_purchase`/`dns_purchase` have zero corpus coverage, so porting the fill would add untested code that the twin gate cannot check. Note the asymmetry this creates — the Python twin's `PORTED_BTYPES` set skips the same btypes, so the gate cannot detect a MISSING fill at all. Coverage of the fill set is a human responsibility, not a gated one.

runs.note: The composite-reuse rule in one row: thirteen keys, seven of them null, because the claim only has a side-1. Keys are alphabetical in the output — that is `render_value` sorting, not the `emplace_back` order in the fill. This same fixture also produces a `jetton_transfer` row (the payout leg), which is why the grep filter is needed.

sections.heading: The render seam and the Python parity contract
sections.prose:
`render_action` is the piece that did NOT move lib-side, and the split is exactly where you would want it: everything above produces an `Action` value; this turns one into a line of text for the A/B channel. Production never calls it — it binds the same `Action` to SQL instead ([[prod-path]]).

The parity contract is stronger than it is for any other layer in this engine. `twins/py_actions.py` does not reimplement the serializer — it calls the REAL `block_tree_serializer.block_to_action` and renders the result in this same column set. So a diff here is a diff against production Python, not against a twin's approximation.

annotations.text: The row is rendered by building a `Value` Dict and handing it to the ordinary `render_value`. That is why an Action row and a block's `data` render with identical syntax — one renderer, so a `str:`/`amount:`/`cellhash:` prefix means the same thing everywhere in the dumps.

`tx_hashes` and `accounts` are sorted HERE, at render time, not in `build_action`. The reason is Python: `list(set(...))` gives hash order, so neither side has a meaningful order to compare. Sorting at the boundary keeps the diff stable without forcing an order the data model does not have.

The eight directional columns pass through as raw `Value`s — no conversion left to do, because `av_addr` already ran inside the fill. If one of these ever renders as `asset:…` or `0:ABC…` (an Account) instead of `str:0:ABC…`, a fill skipped its converter.

What is absent is as informative as what is present: no `trace_id`, no `trace_end_lt`/`trace_*`, no `finality`, and no roles. The trace-level fields are constant per fixture (the twin feeds a stub Trace), and roles do not exist on this branch — so neither is gated here, and neither should be inferred from this list.

excerpts.title: run_dump — where the two dump modes diverge

annotations.text: The failure line goes to stdout as a bare `TRACE_FAIL` while the REASON goes to stderr. That asymmetry is deliberate: stdout is the byte-compared channel, and exception messages are the one thing that will never match between a C++ and a Python engine.

Fallback rows are tagged `FALLBACK` and only exist in `--actions` mode; `--classify` prints nothing after a TRACE_FAIL. Since no corpus trace fails, this entire block is dead in every gate run — which is precisely why the tag exists, so that if it ever fires it is unmistakable in a diff.

The two modes share everything up to this point and differ only in the per-action render: `build_action` + `render_action` for `--actions`, `emit_action` (raw block data) for `--classify`. Note the `continue` on a false return — an unported btype is skipped SILENTLY, so `--classify` and `--actions` row counts can legitimately differ. Today they don't (199 = 199).

Every field of every row above — ids, lt windows, sorted tx_hashes and accounts, every composite key — is byte-identical to what `block_tree_serializer.block_to_action` produces in the real Python classifier. The mechanics of the gate set (and the other five twins) are [[gates]].

sections.heading: Check yourself
sections.prose:
Four things worth doing before moving on to [[gates]]. The first has its captured output below; the other three you run yourself.

2. Prove that composite key ORDER is not gated. Swap any two adjacent `f.emplace_back(...)` lines inside `fill_jetton_transfer` (`ActionBuild.cpp` 105-113), rebuild `ton-mch-engine`, and re-run the twin diff from the previous section. It stays at 0, because `render_value` sorts keys. Then convince yourself why that is still dangerous: the DB composite in `indexer/core/database.py` is positional.

3. Prove that field VALUES are gated, hard. Swap `a.source` and `a.destination` in the same fill, rebuild, re-run the diff — you should see roughly 114 changed rows (one per jetton_transfer in the histogram above), and the ids will NOT change, because `action_id` is derived from the event node and the btype, never from the columns. That is worth seeing once: a corrupted row keeps its identity.

4. Read `block_to_action`'s tail in `indexer/indexer/events/blocks/utils/block_tree_serializer.py` (lines 1519-1541) next to `build_action`'s tail (`ActionBuild.cpp` 595-622) and check the four accounts sources line up: event-node tx accounts, source + source_secondary, destination pair gated on `is_ghost_block`, and the initiating tx's account gated on `is_tick_tock`. If you can also say why Python's `list(set(...))` there forces both dumps to sort, you have the parity contract.

runs.note: Then read `indexer/core/database.py` around line 241: `ActionAccount` is `(action_id, trace_id, account)` plus four lt/utime denorm columns — no role, no `account_roles`. If you have read a description of `ROLE_SENDER`/`ROLE_RECEIVER` for this codebase, it was about a different branch, and `Action.accounts` being a bare string list here is the deliberate consequence.
